resources.string: LTE
Long Term Evolution, the 4G mobile network. Most mobile data still travels over LTE, including the LTE \"anchor\" that 5G NSA is built on.
LTE+
LTE with carrier aggregation: the phone is using several LTE channels at once, which gives more speed than plain LTE. It is still 4G.
Carrier aggregation
Combining two or more radio channels into one connection, so data can flow over all of them at once. Shown as LTE+ in the status bar.
LTE-A Pro
LTE Advanced Pro, the last upgrade to 4G: more aggregated channels and smarter antennas. Some US carriers call it \"5G E\", but it is LTE, not 5G.
5G
The fifth generation of mobile networks. Its radio is called NR. The label after it says how the phone is using it: NSA (alongside LTE) or SA (5G on its own).
5G on spectrum the carrier treats as its fastest, usually high band (mmWave) or very wide channels. Speeds can be much higher, but range is shorter.
NR
New Radio, the radio technology 5G uses. \"LTE + NR\" means the phone has an LTE connection with 5G NR added on top.
NSA

Non-standalone 5G. The phone stays connected to an LTE cell, which handles signalling, and 5G NR is added for extra speed. Android may show 5G when the LTE cell only offers 5G nearby, even if no data is going over NR at that moment.
SA
Standalone 5G. The phone talks to a 5G core network over NR alone, with no LTE underneath. It can mean lower latency and newer 5G features.
High band
High-frequency 5G spectrum, such as mmWave. Very fast but short range, and easily blocked by walls. Carriers often label it 5G+ or 5G UW.
3G
The third generation of mobile networks (UMTS, HSPA). Usable data but slow by today\'s standards. Many carriers have switched it off.
2G
The second generation of mobile networks (GSM, GPRS, EDGE). Calls and texts, but very slow data.
eSIM
An embedded SIM: a chip built into the phone that is set up by downloading a profile from the carrier, instead of inserting a plastic card.
Wi-Fi
The phone is reaching the internet over Wi-Fi right now, so mobile data is not being used, even though a SIM is set for mobile data.
VPN
A virtual private network. Your traffic is tunnelled through a VPN app, on top of Wi-Fi or mobile data.
Cellular
Mobile data from a SIM. The phone uses it when it isn\'t connected to Wi-Fi (or Wi-Fi has no internet). The tiles below show which SIM is carrying it.
Wi-Fi 7
802.11be, the newest Wi-Fi generation. It can use very wide channels and several bands at once, for the highest speeds and lowest latency. Both the phone and router must support it.
Wi-Fi 6E
Wi-Fi 6 on the 6 GHz band. The extra spectrum is less crowded, so it\'s often faster and steadier, but 6 GHz doesn\'t reach as far through walls.
Wi-Fi 6
802.11ax. Faster than Wi-Fi 5 and much better when lots of devices share one network.
Wi-Fi 5
802.11ac, on the 5 GHz band. Still common and fast enough for most uses.
Wi-Fi 4
802.11n, an older generation. It works on 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz but is noticeably slower than Wi-Fi 5 or 6.
Older Wi-Fi

Wi-Fi 1, 2 and 3 are the original 802.11b, 802.11a and 802.11g standards, from around 1999 to 2003. Much slower than anything since. The Android emulator\'s virtual Wi-Fi also reports itself this way.
WPA3
The newest Wi-Fi security. It protects the password against guessing attacks and keeps past traffic safe even if the password later leaks.
WPA2
Wi-Fi Protected Access 2, the most common Wi-Fi security. Fine with a strong password; WPA3 is newer and stronger.
WEP
A very old Wi-Fi security scheme that can be broken in minutes. Treat the network as open.
Open
No Wi-Fi password or encryption. Others nearby can see your traffic unless the app or website encrypts it (most do, over HTTPS).
Enhanced Open
No password, but each device\'s traffic is still encrypted (OWE), so others nearby can\'t read it.
